title: Let the dead bury their dead (Matthew 8:14–22)
word: Let the dead bury their dead
hook: a hard saying: following doesn't wait for a convenient time
tomorrow: what kind of person does a storm obey?

segments.voice: Last week ended at a wide table: many shall come from east and west. Now, a long day in Capernaum, and two people who want to follow.
screen: `MANY SHALL COME FROM EAST AND WEST.` → `A LONG DAY IN CAPERNAUM.`

segments.voice: Calendars fill up with afters: after exams, after the move, after things settle down. Capernaum, evening. Jesus has just healed Peter's mother-in-law: "He touched her hand, and the fever left her: and she arose, and ministered unto them." A crowd has come with their sick, and he heals them. Now he gives the word to cross the lake, and two men step up to follow. One of them has a request that couldn't sound more reasonable. It's about a funeral.
screen: `AFTER THINGS SETTLE DOWN.` → `THE FEVER LEFT HER.` → `TWO MEN STEP UP.`

segments.voice: The first is a scribe, a teacher of the law, all promise: "Master, I will follow thee whithersoever thou goest." Jesus doesn't turn him away. He tells him the cost: "The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Then a disciple: "Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father." It sounds completely fair. The commandments say, "Honour thy father and thy mother." And Jesus answers: "Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead." Matthew doesn't explain it, and readers differ. Some think the father hadn't died yet, and the man meant someday, once he's gone. Some hear the first dead as people dead to God's call, burying their own. Some hear a deliberate shock, said to wake him. Notice the word first in the man's request, and the two words Jesus begins with: follow me. Not when things settle. Now. It's said to one man at one moment; Matthew doesn't make it a rule about funerals, or about grief. But it sits right beside the scribe who promised too much too fast, and both get the same answer: the real cost, in the present tense.
screen: `THE SCRIBE: WHITHERSOEVER.` · `THE FOXES HAVE HOLES.` · `SUFFER ME FIRST.` · `FOLLOW ME, NOW.` · then, large: `FOLLOW NOW.`

segments.voice: Pick up your phone and find the message you keep meaning to send: the thank-you, the check-in, the apology sitting in drafts. Send it now, or, if now truly isn't right, set it to go at the first moment it can. Then put the phone face down and rest.
Let the dead bury their dead. A hard saying with more than one reading, and one plain center: follow me.
screen: `LET THE DEAD BURY THEIR DEAD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this one: follow now, not after things settle, and not some better day. Sleep well.

screen: `DAY 1436 COUNTS.` → `MATTHEW, READ THROUGH · 10 OF 60.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT KIND OF PERSON DOES A STORM OBEY?`

howItsDone: Some Christians treat the call to follow me as daily and present, and in some traditions people answer it with a fresh start each morning rather than waiting for a better time.

notes: Three readings of 'let the dead bury their dead' (the father not yet dead; the spiritually dead burying their own; a deliberate shock) are given as 'some', without ranking. Confirm they are fair.
'It's said to one man, at one moment; Matthew doesn't make it a rule about funerals' is added so grieving listeners don't hear a rule against mourning; confirm.
The KJV of 8:15 begins 'And he touched her hand'; the voice quotes from 'He touched'. Confirm.
'When evening comes, they bring him many more' paraphrases 8:16 ('When the even was come, they brought unto him many').
'A scribe, a teacher of the law' is a plain gloss; confirm.
